A drawer holds 4 red and 4 blue socks. It is dark, so you cannot see colours. What is the fewest socks you must pull out to be sure you have two of the same colour?
Try the worst case: what if you are unlucky every time?
Two socks can be different colours. What happens with the third one?
Imagine bad luck: the first sock is red and the second is blue.
The third sock is red or blue – and it always pairs with one of the first two.
So 3 socks are enough. Mathematicians call this the pigeonhole principle.

Among 9 coins one is fake – it is lighter. You have a balance scale with no weights. How many weighings are enough to surely find the fake?
What if you split the coins into groups of three and compare two groups?
After the first weighing you know which group of three holds the fake. How do you find it among three coins?
Split the coins into 3 groups and weigh two groups. The lighter side – or balance – tells you which group has the fake.
Weigh two coins from that group: the lighter is fake, and if they balance, the third is.
Two weighings in total are enough.
